title: Thin walls flute longitudinally; thick narrow necks pleat transversely

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Thin walls flute longitudinally; thick narrow necks pleat transversely

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Small tension changes in a thin-walled elongated cell produce wrinkling in the plane of greatest curvature, hence longitudinal fluting, especially near the ends; where the wall is thick relative to diameter, as in the narrow neck of Lagena or tubular hydroid gonangia, bending stiffness makes folding transverse instead.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: The manner in which our little Lagena-shell tends to fold or wrinkle, longitudinally in its wider part, and transversely or annularly in its narrow neck, is thus completely and easily explained.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter V, “The Forms of Cells”; topic “Wrinkling and fluting of shells”. Scope: Lagena and other foraminifera, campanularian gonangia, and similar thin-walled elongated organic vesicles

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch05-21: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.60

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The geometric prediction is precise and modern shell-buckling models provide discriminating alternatives. Public morphology can test wrinkle orientation in subsets, but thickness and loading data needed for the proposed mechanism are often absent.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: From 3D shell and gonangium images, relate wrinkle orientation to local curvature, diameter, and wall-thickness ratio and compare the observed transition with elastic-shell buckling predictions.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Available scans cover only a subset of the stated taxa.

Wall thickness and in-vivo tension are seldom recorded.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.35
operationalizability: 0.86
data existence: 0.48
analysis feasibility: 0.64
discriminating power: 0.7

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Fold direction and chamber proportions are visible on existing Lagena plates, and the predicted switch from longitudinal to transverse folds is a sharp pattern. Thickness, the variable that is supposed to cause the switch, is only sporadically available, and the non-foraminiferal cases in the claim are uncompiled. The association can be tested for Lagena more readily than for the full scope.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: On Lagena and similar elongated vesicles, measure wall thickness relative to local diameter and the direction of folds. Longitudinal flutes on thin, strongly curved regions and transverse pleats on thick narrow necks would support the claim; the opposite pattern, or no association, would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Genetic ornament can imitate mechanical wrinkles, and hydroid gonangia are not in the foraminiferal archives.

Most catalog images do not report wall thickness, so the stiffness variable has to be inferred or measured from a subset of sections and micro-CT.
